home.title: Free speech therapy games for kids – Chatterbox
home.description: Chatterbox: free speech, reading and maths games for children aged 4–12, with a friendly animal who talks and listens. No ads, and it works offline.
home.h1: Chatterbox: free speech, reading and maths games for kids
home.lead: A friendly animal companion who talks and listens, and a few minutes a day of speech, reading and maths. Free, with no ads, for children aged 4–12.

sections.html:
Lots of parents look for free speech therapy games for kids – something useful between appointments, or simply better than another cartoon. Chatterbox is home practice in that spirit: a web game where a friendly animal says every task out loud, and the microphone hears when your child answers.

Each day brings short Speech, Reading and Maths lessons, a few minutes each. Your child earns stars, keeps a day streak going and collects medals and achievements, so practice feels like play rather than homework.

It runs in the browser on any phone, tablet or laptop, works offline after the first launch, and has no ads and nothing to buy.

Chatterbox is for children aged 4 to 12. There’s a younger track for ages 4–6 and an older track for 7 and up, so it works as one of your learning games for 5 year olds and still has plenty for a ten-year-old. For children growing up in several languages, there’s a My languages section – more in our guide to {{page:world|multilingual children}}.

Your child picks their interests – racing, chess, K-pop, football, animals, drawing and more – and the game adapts to them. Then they choose a friend: a tiger, kitten, panda, unicorn, ghost, koala, alpaca or red panda.

• Speech: tongue warm-ups with pictures that show where the tongue goes, breathing exercises, tongue twisters and chants, and games for the R, L, S, Z and SH sounds.
  • Reading: letters, “sound trains” that join letters together, Read and find, colour-by-letter colouring pages and a reading diary for your child’s own book.
  • Maths: an abacus for mental arithmetic for little ones, Step by Step (20 timed steps from counting dots to equations) and olympiad problems for ages 8+.
  • Chess: 10 levels against the computer, with a coach and hints.
  • The L track: a motorbike race where reading words aloud fires the nitro, with tricks, a garage and coins.
  • And more: the World Museum (1,000 famous paintings with a guide for kids), fun composers and their music, songs, a xylophone, drawing, playground physics experiments and more.

1. Open {{play|Chatterbox}} in your browser.
  2. Let your child choose a friend and a few interests.
  3. Play the first lessons together.
  4. Add Chatterbox to your home screen so it’s one tap away, even offline.

Want the stars to follow your child from the tablet to your phone? Turn on the family login.

The family shares one login with a password of 4 pictures (each picture stands for a digit). On any device, everyone taps themselves on Who’s playing? Children get their own game and stars; grandparents get their own screen with the week’s progress, praise and chess. More in {{page:grand|Chatterbox for grandparents}}.

Brothers and sisters can take each other on in the family league and battles, or keep a team streak going together.

• A family control panel, locked with a code on your child’s phone.
  • Progress stays on the device. It’s stored on the server (Cloudflare) only if you turn on the family login, and you can delete it from the control panel.
  • No ads, no tracking, no purchases.

Chatterbox is home practice: it’s not a diagnosis and not a replacement for a speech and language therapist (SLT). Our guides cover the {{page:r|R sound}}, the {{page:l|L sound}}, {{page:s|S, Z and SH}}, {{page:gym|tongue exercises}} and {{page:read|learning to read with phonics}}.

faq.q: Is Chatterbox really free?
faq.a: Yes. There are no ads, no purchases and nothing to unlock.

faq.q: What age is it for?
faq.a: Children aged 4–12. There’s a younger track for ages 4–6 and an older track for 7 and up, and the game adapts to the interests your child picks.

faq.q: Do I need to install anything?
faq.a: No. Chatterbox runs in the browser on any phone, tablet or laptop. You can add it to your home screen like an app, and after the first launch it works offline.

faq.q: Why does it use the microphone?
faq.a: The friendly animal says every task aloud, and the microphone hears when your child speaks – so your child practises talking out loud, not just tapping.

faq.q: Can it replace a speech therapist?
faq.a: No. Chatterbox is home practice, not a diagnosis and not a replacement for a speech and language therapist. If you’re worried about your child’s speech, please talk to an SLT.

faq.q: Can grandparents join in?
faq.a: Yes. With the family login, grandparents tap themselves on “Who’s playing?” and get their own screen with the week’s progress, praise, chess and the grandchildren’s games. See {{page:grand|the page for grandparents}}.

r.title: How to help my child say the R sound: a parent’s guide
r.description: When the R sound usually arrives, why children say W instead, when to see a speech and language therapist, plus warm-ups, simple steps and games.
r.h1: How to help your child say the R sound
r.lead: Plenty of children say “wabbit” for “rabbit” for quite a while. Here’s what’s typical, when to ask a speech and language therapist, and gentle ways to practise at home.

sections.h2: When does the R sound usually arrive?
sections.html:
R is one of the last English sounds to settle. Between about 3 and 5, lots of children swap it for W: “wed” for “red”, “wing” for “ring”. Most children say R clearly by about 5–6, though some take a little longer, so treat ages as a rough guide rather than a deadline.

A note on accents: in many accents in England, R is only heard before a vowel – in red, carrot or tree, but not at the end of car. That’s where practice starts. In Irish, Scottish and North American accents the R in car is pronounced too; work on it once the R at the start of words is easy.

sections.h2: When to see a speech and language therapist
sections.html:
Trust your instincts. It’s worth asking a speech and language therapist (SLT) if:

  • your child is around 6 or older and still says W for R most of the time;
  • other sounds are missing too, or people outside the family find your child hard to understand;
  • your child is upset about it, avoids talking or is being teased;
  • you have any concerns about hearing, or about how freely the tongue moves.

Your GP, health visitor, nursery or school can point you to local speech and language therapy. An early check never hurts, even if the answer is “give it time”.

A minute or two of play gets the mouth and ears ready. These are warm-ups, not a cure: real progress comes from practising the sound itself.

  • Tiger growl: a long, low “grrrr”. The back of the tongue lifts, close to where R is made.
  • Paint the ceiling: mouth open, the tongue tip slides back along the roof of the mouth. 5 strokes.
  • Smile and kiss: a wide smile, then a kiss, 5 times – so your child feels the difference between relaxed lips and rounded lips.

More ideas in our guide to {{page:gym|tongue exercises for speech}}.

sections.h2: Step by step: from listening to talking
sections.html:
1. Listen first. Use pairs of words that differ only in R and W: ring/wing, red/wed, rake/wake, right/white. You say one; your child points to the right picture. Children need to hear the difference before they can make it.
  2. Find the sound. Keep the lips relaxed (a kiss shape turns R into W) and let the sides of the tongue touch the top back teeth. From a growly “grrr” or a long “eee”, slide into “rrr”. A mirror helps.
  3. Syllables: ra, ree, roo, ro.
  4. Words: R at the start (red, rabbit, rain, rocket), then in the middle (carrot, berry, giraffe), then in blends (tree, green, brick, frog).
  5. Phrases and sentences: “a red rocket”, “Run, rabbit, run!”
  6. Everyday talk: choose one moment a day – snack time, the walk to school – to listen out for good Rs.

Stay on each step until it’s easy; if things get wobbly, go back one. Five minutes a day beats an hour on Saturday.

sections.h2: Games that make R practice fun
sections.html:
• Racing engines: start the engine with a long “rrrrr” before every turn of a board game.
  • Ring or wing? Draw a ring and a wing. Take turns to say one word while the other points. When a “wing” gets the ring, it’s funny – and shows why the sound matters.
  • R treasure hunt: find five things at home that start with R – a rubber, a ruler, a rug…
  • Rhyme time: rain, train, drain – who can find the most?

In {{play|Chatterbox}}, a friendly animal says every task aloud and the microphone hears when your child answers. The Speech lessons include tongue warm-ups with pictures that show where the tongue goes, breathing exercises, tongue twisters and chants, and games for the R sound – a few minutes a day, with stars and streaks to keep things going.

• “No, not wabbit!” Instead, repeat it back correctly: “Yes, a rabbit! A fluffy rabbit.” This is called modelling, and it teaches without pressure.
  • Drilling one word again and again until your child gets cross.
  • Correcting in front of others. Keep practice private.
  • Rushing to sentences before the sound is steady in single words.
  • Long sessions. Little and often works better.
  • Waiting and worrying. If you’re unsure, ask an SLT.

faq.q: Is saying W instead of R normal?
faq.a: Yes, it’s very common between about 3 and 5. Most children say R clearly by about 5–6, and some take a little longer. If your child is around 6 or older and still uses W most of the time, ask a speech and language therapist.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn the R sound?
faq.a: It varies a lot – from a few weeks to several months. Short daily practice and lots of modelling help. If there’s no progress after a few months of regular practice, an SLT can work out why.

faq.q: Can tongue exercises fix the R sound on their own?
faq.a: No. They’re a fun warm-up, but children learn R by hearing it, finding it and practising it in syllables, words and sentences.

faq.q: Should I correct my child every time?
faq.a: No. Repeat the word back correctly and carry on the conversation. Save focused practice for a few minutes a day.

l.title: L sound activities for kids: practise at home
l.description: Easy L sound activities for children: when L usually develops, why kids say W or Y instead, when to see an SLT, plus warm-ups, steps and games.
l.h1: L sound activities: helping your child say L
l.lead: “Yeyyow” for “yellow” or “wion” for “lion”? That’s very common in young children. Here’s what’s typical, and how to practise the L sound at home a few minutes at a time.

sections.h2: When does the L sound usually develop?
sections.html:
Most children are saying L clearly somewhere between 4 and 6. Before that, it’s common to hear it swapped for W (“wion” for “lion”) or Y (“yeyyow” for “yellow”). Every child is different, so treat ages as a rough guide, not a deadline.

A note on accents: in many British accents, the L at the end of words like ball, milk or table naturally sounds a bit like a W or an “oo”. That’s accent, not a speech difficulty. Focus on L at the start of words and between vowels: lion, leaf, lolly, yellow.

sections.h2: When to talk to a speech and language therapist
sections.html:
Ask a speech and language therapist (SLT) if:

  • your child is around 6 and still replaces L most of the time;
  • several sounds are unclear, or your child is hard to understand;
  • the tongue can’t easily lift to the top teeth, or you’ve wondered about tongue-tie;
  • your child gets frustrated, avoids words or is teased.

Your GP, health visitor, nursery or school can tell you how to reach local services. It’s fine to ask “just to check”.

sections.h2: Where the tongue goes, and a quick warm-up
sections.html:
For L, the tip of the tongue lifts and touches the bumpy ridge just behind the top front teeth, and the sound flows out around the sides. The lips stay relaxed: if they round into a kiss, you’ll hear a W. Practise in front of a mirror so your child can see the tongue go up.

  • Tongue tap: mouth slightly open, tap the tip on the ridge behind the top teeth: “la-la-la”. 10 taps.
  • Ice-lolly lick: pretend to lick an ice lolly from bottom to top. 5 licks.
  • Lift and hold: tongue tip up behind the top teeth, hold for 5 seconds, relax. 5 times.
  • Lip lick: lick the top lip slowly from corner to corner. 5 times.

More in {{page:gym|tongue exercises for speech}}. Keep warm-ups short and silly: they get the tongue moving, but they’re not the practice itself.

1. Listening: play with pairs like light/white, lake/wake and lock/wok, or let/yet, less/yes and lawn/yawn. You say a word; your child points to the picture.
  2. The sound alone: a long, singing “lllll” with the tongue tip up.
  3. Syllables: la, lee, loo, lo – then “lalala”, “lololo”.
  4. Words: L at the start (lion, leg, lemon, lolly), then in the middle (balloon, jelly, yellow), then in blends (play, blue, clock, flag).
  5. Phrases: “lots of lemons”, “a lovely blue balloon”.
  6. Everyday talk: pick one routine – bath time, the bus – for listening out for L.

Stay on each step until it’s easy. If it gets wobbly, go back one step; that’s part of learning.

• La-la karaoke: sing a favourite song using only “la”.
  • Lock or wok? Draw a lock and a wok. Take turns saying one while the other points. Mix-ups are funny, and they show why the sound matters.
  • L spotting: on a walk, look for things that start with L – leaves, lorries, lamp posts, ladders.
  • Lolly shop: make paper lollies and “sell” them; your child orders a lemon, lime or lychee lolly.
  • Tongue twisters: “lovely lemon lollies” – for later, once L is steady in words.

The L track in {{play|Chatterbox}} is a motorbike race: reading words aloud fires the nitro, and there are tricks, a garage and coins to collect. The Speech lessons add tongue warm-ups with pictures of the tongue position, tongue twisters and chants. A friendly animal says every task aloud, and the microphone hears when your child speaks.

• “Say it properly!” Model it instead: “Yes, a lion! A big lion.”
  • Long sessions. 5–10 minutes a day is plenty.
  • Worrying about the L in ball if that’s simply how your accent sounds.
  • Jumping to sentences before single words are steady.

faq.q: My child says “yeyyow” for “yellow”. Is that normal?
faq.a: Yes, swapping L for Y or W is common in young children. Most say L clearly somewhere between 4 and 6. If your child is around 6 and still swaps it most of the time, ask an SLT.

faq.q: My child’s tongue pokes out between the teeth for L. Does it matter?
faq.a: If the L sounds clear, it often settles on its own. If the tongue also comes forward for S and Z, or you’re unsure, ask a speech and language therapist.

faq.q: How often should we practise?
faq.a: A few minutes every day works better than a long session once a week. Stop while it’s still fun.

faq.q: Are L sound activities enough on their own?
faq.a: For many children, play and modelling are all it takes. If there’s little progress after a few months, or other sounds are unclear too, get an SLT’s opinion.

s.title: Lisp exercises for kids: S, Z and SH sounds
s.description: Lisp exercises for kids: frontal and lateral lisps, when S, Z and SH usually settle, when to see a speech and language therapist, plus easy games.
s.h1: S, Z and SH sounds: lisp exercises for kids
s.lead: “Thun” for “sun”, a slushy S, or “sip” for “ship”? Here’s what’s typical, which lisp is worth a check, and simple ways to practise at home.

sections.h2: Lisps and SH swaps: what you might hear
sections.html:
• Frontal (interdental) lisp: the tongue pokes between the teeth, so S sounds like TH – “thun” for “sun” – and Z like the TH in “this”. Very common in young children.
  • Lateral lisp: the air escapes over the sides of the tongue, giving a wet, slushy S, a bit like the Welsh “ll”. This isn’t a usual stage of development.
  • SH replaced by S: “sip” for “ship”, “sue” for “shoe”. Common while SH is still developing.

Z is S with the voice switched on, so it usually follows S.

sections.h2: What’s typical, and when to see an SLT
sections.html:
Many children have a frontal lisp when they’re small, and it often fades by about 5. SH usually comes along by about 5–6, sometimes a little later. Around 6–7, when the front baby teeth fall out, S can turn whistly or lispy for a while; that usually settles once the new teeth grow in.

Ask a speech and language therapist (SLT) if:

  • you hear a lateral lisp at any age – it’s worth a check rather than waiting;
  • a frontal lisp is still there after about 5 and isn’t fading;
  • your child is 6 or older and SH is still missing;
  • your child is hard to understand, or unhappy about their speech.

sections.h2: Warm-ups for S, Z and SH
sections.html:
• Teeth fence: smile with the teeth gently together; the tongue hides behind the “fence”. Hold for 5 seconds, 5 times.
  • Snake: through the smile, let out a long, thin “sssss”. Hold a finger in front of the middle of the lips: the cool air should come out right there, not from the sides.
  • Bee: same position, voice on: “zzzzz”. Feel the buzz on the throat.
  • Quiet please: for SH, push the lips forward like a trumpet and pull the tongue a little further back: “shhhh”.
  • Feather blow: blow a feather or a scrap of tissue across the table with one steady stream of air.

These are playful warm-ups, not a lisp treatment on their own. For more, see {{page:gym|tongue exercises for speech}}.

1. Listen: use minimal pairs – sea/she, sip/ship, sock/shock, save/shave for SH; sink/think, sum/thumb, mouse/mouth for a frontal lisp. You say one; your child points to the picture.
  2. Find the sound: tongue behind the teeth. A handy trick for S: say a quiet “t” and stretch it into “t-sssss”. For SH, lips forward like a trumpet.
  3. Syllables: sa, see, soo; sha, shee, shoo.
  4. Words: at the start (sun, sock, zoo, shoe, ship), at the end (bus, house, buzz, fish, wish), then in the middle (pencil, dinosaur, washing). Some children find the end of a word easiest – start wherever it works.
  5. Sentences: “Six silly snakes”, then “She sells seashells” once both sounds are steady.
  6. Everyday talk: listen out for S or SH during one routine a day.

sections.h2: Games for S, Z and SH
sections.html:
• Snake or bee? Point to a snake picture for “sss” and a bee for “zzz”, switching faster and faster.
  • Sea or she? Take turns saying one word while the other points. Mix-ups get a laugh.
  • Shopping list: collect things with S or SH around the house – soap, socks, shampoo, shoes.
  • Steam train: “shh-shh-shh” as a train chugs round the room; it stops when the driver says “sss”.

{{play|Chatterbox}} has games for the S, Z and SH sounds, tongue warm-ups with pictures that show where the tongue should be, breathing exercises, and tongue twisters and chants. A friendly animal reads every task aloud and the microphone hears when your child speaks – a few minutes a day, with stars and streaks.

• Waiting on a lateral lisp. Get it checked by an SLT.
  • “Stop lisping!” Modelling the word clearly works better than pointing out the mistake.
  • Too long, too serious. A few minutes, lots of fun.
  • Tongue twisters too early. Get single words steady first.

faq.q: Is a lisp normal at 4?
faq.a: A frontal lisp (tongue between the teeth) is common at that age and often fades by about 5. A lateral, slushy-sounding lisp is worth checking with a speech and language therapist at any age.

faq.q: Can lisp exercises for kids fix a lisp at home?
faq.a: For a mild frontal lisp, short daily listening and practice often help. Warm-ups alone won’t do it, and a lateral lisp is best looked at by an SLT.

faq.q: My 6-year-old’s S went funny when the front teeth fell out. Should I worry?
faq.a: Usually not: gaps make S harder for a while, and it tends to settle once the new teeth come through. If it doesn’t, ask an SLT.

faq.q: Why does my child say “sue” for “shoe”?
faq.a: SH develops later than S for many children, often by about 5–6. Listening games with pairs like sea/she help your child hear the difference first.

gym.title: Tongue exercises for speech: fun warm-ups for kids
gym.description: Tongue exercises for speech, explained for parents: how to do them with a mirror in 5–7 minutes a day, 12 classic warm-ups, and what they can’t do.
gym.h1: Tongue exercises for speech: fun warm-ups for kids
gym.lead: Pancakes, snakes and galloping horses: classic tongue and lip exercises make a playful warm-up before speech practice. Here’s how to do them, and what to expect.

sections.h2: What tongue exercises can and can’t do
sections.html:
Tongue and lip exercises – sometimes called oral motor exercises or oral motor play – help a child notice their tongue, move it on purpose and get ready to talk. They’re fun, and they make a good warm-up.

But it’s worth being realistic: on their own, they don’t teach a new sound. Children learn sounds by hearing them, trying them and practising them in words. So treat these exercises as a two-minute warm-up before you work on {{page:r|the R sound}}, {{page:l|the L sound}} or {{page:s|S and SH}} – not as the main event, and not as a cure.

• Use a mirror. Sit side by side so your child can see you both. You go first; they copy.
  • 5–7 minutes a day. Short and regular beats long and rare.
  • Slow and steady. Repeat each movement about 5 times, or hold it for about 5 seconds.
  • Stop while it’s fun. If your child is tired or cross, call it a day.
  • Never force. Don’t move your child’s tongue with fingers or spoons. If something is too hard, skip it.
  • Make it a story. “The tongue wakes up, makes a pancake, then goes for a ride on a horse…”

1. Smile and kiss: a wide smile (hold for 5 seconds), then push the lips forward into a kiss (5 seconds). Swap 5 times.
  2. Pancake: open the mouth and rest a wide, relaxed, flat tongue on the bottom lip. Hold for 5 seconds, 3–5 times.
  3. Snake: make the tongue narrow and pointy, poke it out, then pull it back in. 5 times.
  4. Clock: mouth open, the tongue tip touches one corner of the mouth, then the other: tick, tock. 10 times, slowly.
  5. Lick the jam: lick round the lips in a slow circle, one way and then the other. 3 circles each way.
  6. Up and down: mouth open, the tongue tip reaches up to the top lip, then down to the bottom lip. 5 times.
  7. Paint the ceiling: mouth open, the tongue tip “paints” the roof of the mouth from just behind the top teeth backwards. 5–8 strokes.
  8. Horse: click the tongue against the roof of the mouth: clip-clop, clip-clop. 10 clicks.
  9. Brush the teeth: lips closed, the tongue tip runs along the front of the top teeth, then the bottom teeth, behind the lips. 3 times each.
  10. Sticky tongue: press the whole tongue up against the roof of the mouth, then open the mouth wide without letting go. Hold for 3–5 seconds. It’s tricky, and fine if it doesn’t work yet.
  11. Balloon cheeks: puff up both cheeks, hold for 3 seconds, then gently pop them. Then puff one cheek at a time.
  12. Fish face: suck the cheeks in to make a fish face, hold for 3 seconds, relax. 5 times.

A long, steady stream of air helps with sounds like S and SH. Try:

  • Bubbles: a slow, gentle blow makes the biggest bubble.
  • Cotton-wool football: blow a cotton-wool ball across the table into a goal, with or without a straw.
  • Feather float: keep a feather in the air for as long as you can.
  • Smell the flower, blow out the candle: breathe in through the nose, then out slowly through the mouth at a pretend candle.

Keep breathing games short – a few blows, then a rest – so nobody gets dizzy.

1. Smile and kiss – 5 times.
  2. Pancake and snake – 3 of each.
  3. Clock – 10 ticks.
  4. Paint the ceiling – 5 strokes.
  5. Horse – 10 clicks.
  6. Cotton-wool football – one goal.
  7. Then 2–3 minutes on the sound your child is learning.

Talk to a speech and language therapist (SLT) if your child finds most of these movements very hard, still dribbles a lot after about 4, has trouble chewing or swallowing, or can’t lift the tongue or poke it out past the lips – sometimes a sign of tongue-tie, which your GP or health visitor can check. And if a sound isn’t coming along despite regular practice, an SLT can work out why.

In {{play|Chatterbox}}, the Speech lessons include tongue exercises with pictures that show the tongue position, breathing exercises, tongue twisters and chants, and games for the R, L, S, Z and SH sounds. A friendly animal says each task aloud, so your child can follow along while you keep them company.

faq.q: From what age can children do tongue exercises?
faq.a: Most children can copy simple ones from about 3 or 4. Younger ones simply enjoy pulling faces in the mirror with you, which is fine too.

faq.q: Will tongue exercises fix a lisp or the R sound?
faq.a: Not on their own. They’re a warm-up; sounds are learned by listening and practising them in syllables, words and sentences.

faq.q: How long should we do them for?
faq.a: About 5–7 minutes a day, ideally at the same time each day, and always stopping while it’s still fun.

faq.q: My child can’t do the sticky tongue. Should I worry?
faq.a: Not on its own – it’s one of the harder ones. If your child struggles to lift or poke out the tongue at all, ask your GP, health visitor or an SLT.

read.title: How to teach a child to read at home: phonics guide
read.description: How to teach a child to read at home with phonics: letter sounds, blending, segmenting, short daily sessions and easy reading games for ages 4–7.
read.h1: How to teach a child to read at home with phonics
read.lead: You don’t need to be a teacher. A few minutes a day of letter sounds, blending and reading together goes a long way for children aged 4–7.

sections.html:
Phonics teaches children that letters stand for sounds, and that sounds join up to make words. Most schools in the UK teach early reading this way, and many schools elsewhere do too, so phonics at home fits with what your child does in class.

  • Letter sounds: knowing that s says “sss” (not “ess”).
  • Blending: joining sounds together to read a word: c-a-t → cat.
  • Segmenting: splitting a word into its sounds to spell it: dog → d-o-g.
  • Tricky words: common words that don’t follow the rules your child knows yet, such as the, said and was.

Most children start to read somewhere between 4 and 7 – a wide, normal range. Good signs: enjoying stories, noticing letters on signs, spotting rhymes and playing with words. If letters don’t click yet, play listening games first: rhymes, clapping out syllables, and “I spy” with sounds.

1. Pure sounds. Say letter sounds short and clean: “mmm”, not “muh”; “t”, not “tuh”. It makes blending much easier.
  2. A few letters at a time. Many phonics programmes start with s, a, t, p, i, n – enough for words like sat, pin and tap. Add a few new sounds each week.
  3. Blending out loud first. Before reading, play “robot talk”: you say “h-a-t”, your child says “hat”.
  4. Read simple words. Three-letter words made from sounds your child knows. Point under each letter, then sweep your finger along to blend.
  5. Two letters, one sound. Next come sh, ch, th, ck, ng, ee, oo.
  6. Segmenting and spelling. Your child says a word, splits it into sounds, then writes it or builds it with magnetic letters.
  7. Short books. Decodable books (from school or the library) use only the sounds your child has learned, so success comes quickly.

If your child is already at school, ask which sounds they’re learning this week and follow the same order.

• 5–10 minutes a day is plenty for a 4- or 5-year-old.
  • Stop while your child still wants more.
  • Read to your child every day as well: stories build vocabulary and a love of books in a way phonics alone can’t.
  • Praise effort: “You worked that out sound by sound!”
  • If your child gets stuck, sound the word out together, then read it again smoothly.

• Sound I spy: “I spy something beginning with mmm.”
  • Robot talk: give instructions in sounds: “Pat the c-a-t”, “Find your h-a-t”.
  • Treasure hunt: hide word cards; each word your child reads points to the next hiding place.
  • Silly sentences: build funny sentences from word cards: “A pig sat on a hat.”
  • Letter hunt: spot today’s letter on cereal boxes, shop signs and number plates.

If reading seems much harder for your child than for classmates, if sounds are still getting mixed up after a year of school, or if your child struggles to hear rhymes or the sounds in words, talk to the class teacher. Hearing and eyesight checks are a sensible first step. Speech and reading are closely linked, so if your child’s speech is unclear too, a speech and language therapist (SLT) can help.

The Reading lessons in {{play|Chatterbox}} take a few minutes a day: letters, “sound trains” that join letters together, Read and find, colour-by-letter colouring pages, and a reading diary for your child’s own book. A friendly animal reads every task aloud, and stars and streaks keep the habit going.

faq.q: What age should a child start learning to read?
faq.a: Most children start somewhere between 4 and 7. Follow your child’s interest, keep it playful, and talk to the teacher if you’re worried.

faq.q: Should I teach letter names or letter sounds first?
faq.a: Sounds first. Children read c-a-t by blending sounds, not by saying “see-ay-tee”. Letter names can come later.

faq.q: My child knows the sounds but can’t blend them. What can I do?
faq.a: That’s very common. Play robot talk out loud, start with two-sound words like a-t and i-n, and keep the sounds short and pure so they join up easily.

faq.q: How long should a reading session be?
faq.a: 5–10 minutes a day is plenty at first. Reading a story together at bedtime counts too.

grand.title: Chatterbox for grandparents: play with grandchildren
grand.description: How grandparents sign in to Chatterbox with the family login, see what the grandchildren did this week, send them praise and play chess together.
grand.lead: See what your grandchildren did this week, send them praise and play chess together – on your own phone, tablet or laptop.

sections.html:
1. Ask your family for the family login and the picture password. The password is 4 pictures – each picture stands for a digit, so there are no letters to type.
  2. Open {{play|Chatterbox}} on your phone, tablet or laptop and choose the family sign-in.
  3. Enter the login and tap the 4 pictures in order.
  4. On the Who’s playing? screen, tap yourself.

Tip: add Chatterbox to your home screen so you can open it like any other app.

Grandparents get their own screen, made for you rather than for the children:

  • what each grandchild did this week;
  • a way to send them praise;
  • chess;
  • the grandchildren’s games, so you can try them yourself.

Chess is a lovely way to spend time together: you can play chess with your grandchildren right inside the app. When they want to practise on their own, there are 10 levels against the computer, with a coach and hints.

Sitting with a younger grandchild? Ask them to show you their Speech or Reading lesson. The friendly animal reads every task aloud, so you don’t need to know the exercises – just listen and cheer.

Brothers and sisters can also compete in the family league and battles, or keep a team streak going together – a good thing to ask about next time you talk.

Praise the effort, not only the result: “You practised every day this week!” means a lot. If a grandchild is working on a tricky sound, there’s no need to correct them – simply say the word clearly yourself when you reply. Our guides to {{page:r|the R sound}} and {{page:read|learning to read}} explain more.

faq.q: I’m not very good with technology. Is it hard?
faq.a: No. There’s one family login and a password of 4 pictures, then you tap yourself on “Who’s playing?”.

faq.q: Do I need my own account?
faq.a: No. The whole family shares one family login, and everyone has their own place on the “Who’s playing?” screen.

faq.q: Does it cost anything?
faq.a: No. Chatterbox is free, with no ads and no purchases.

faq.title: Chatterbox FAQ: privacy, cost, ages and devices
faq.description: Answers about Chatterbox: is it free, what ages it suits, which devices it runs on, offline play, the family login, privacy and deleting your data.
faq.lead: What parents usually ask about Chatterbox, from cost and privacy to the family login.

sections.html:
• A free web game for children aged 4–12: speech, reading, maths and much more.
  • A friendly animal says every task aloud; the microphone hears when your child speaks.
  • No ads, no purchases, no tracking.
  • Works on any phone, tablet or laptop, and offline after the first launch.
  • Home practice – not a diagnosis, and not a replacement for a speech and language therapist.

Ready to try? {{play|Play Chatterbox for free}}.

faq.q: Is Chatterbox really free?
faq.a: Yes. There are no ads, no purchases and nothing to unlock.

faq.q: What ages is it for?
faq.a: Children aged 4–12. There’s a younger track for ages 4–6 and an older track for 7 and up. Your child picks interests such as racing, chess, K-pop, football, animals or drawing, and the game adapts.

faq.q: What does my child actually do in it?
faq.a: Daily Speech, Reading and Maths lessons of a few minutes each, with stars, day streaks, medals and achievements. There’s also chess, the L track motorbike race, the World Museum, music, songs, drawing, playground physics experiments and more.

faq.q: Which sounds does the English version practise?
faq.a: R, L, S, Z and SH, with tongue warm-ups, breathing exercises, tongue twisters, chants and games. Our guides explain how to help at home: {{page:r|R}}, {{page:l|L}} and {{page:s|S, Z and SH}}.

faq.q: Which devices does it work on?
faq.a: Any phone, tablet or laptop with a web browser. You can add Chatterbox to your home screen so it opens like an app.

faq.q: Does it work offline?
faq.a: Yes. After the first launch, Chatterbox works without an internet connection.

faq.q: Which languages is it available in?
faq.a: English, Russian and Portuguese (Portugal). Each version practises the sounds of its own language.

faq.q: Why does it need the microphone?
faq.a: The friendly animal speaks every task aloud, and the microphone hears when your child speaks, so your child practises talking out loud rather than just tapping.

faq.q: How does the family login work?
faq.a: The family shares one login with a password of 4 pictures, where each picture stands for a digit. On any device, everyone taps themselves on “Who’s playing?”: children get their own game with their stars, and grandparents get their own screen. With the login on, stars sync between devices.

faq.q: Do we have to use the family login?
faq.a: No. Without it, your child can still play, and progress simply stays on that device.

faq.q: What data is stored, and where?
faq.a: Progress stays on your device. It’s stored on the server (Cloudflare) only if your family turns on the family login. There are no ads and no tracking.

faq.q: How do I delete our data?
faq.a: Use the family control panel for parents. On a child’s phone it’s locked with a code, so only grown-ups can open it.

faq.q: Can brothers and sisters play together?
faq.a: Yes. There’s a family league, battles between children and a team streak for siblings.

faq.q: Is Chatterbox a replacement for a speech therapist?
faq.a: No. It’s home practice, not a diagnosis and not a replacement for a speech and language therapist (SLT). If you’re worried about your child’s speech, talk to an SLT; your GP, health visitor or your child’s school can point you to one.

world.title: Bilingual children: one language at home, another at school
world.description: Spanish at home, German at school, English with friends? Why mixing languages is normal, and how Chatterbox helps children who live in several languages.
world.h1: Children of the world: one language at home, another at school, a third with friends
world.lead: Many children grow up in several languages at once: one at home, another at nursery or school, sometimes a third with friends. Parents may worry that their child is getting muddled. In fact, this is what normal development looks like for a child who lives in several worlds at once.

sections.html:
A child starts a sentence in one language and finishes it in another, drops a German word into a Russian sentence, or answers in English when you asked in Spanish. This is called code-switching, and it’s a normal part of bilingual development, not a sign of confusion. Your child reaches for the word that’s closest right now – just as adults do after years of living in another country.

Over time, children get better and better at knowing who to speak which language with: Grandma in Turkish, the teacher in German, friends in English. This skill grows on its own, and play and conversation help it grow faster.

sections.h2: What we know about bilingual children
sections.html:
• Bilingualism doesn’t cause speech disorders. If a child has a real difficulty with speech, it shows in all of their languages, and having more than one language isn’t the cause.
  • Vocabulary is split between languages. Some words your child knows only in the home language, others only in the school language. In each language on its own they may know fewer words than a child of the same age with one language, but count the languages together and the total is no smaller.
  • A silent period is normal. When they start nursery or school in a new language, many children listen and stay quiet at first. This can last a few weeks or months.
  • The home language needs support. Once school starts, the language of the country quickly takes over. The home language stays alive when there’s something to do in it: talking, reading, playing, calling the grandparents.

• Agree on which language goes where. For example: the home language at home and with the grandparents, the local language at school, whatever works with friends. Clear rules make it easier for children.
  • Don’t shame the mixing. If your child slips in a word from another language, simply say the whole sentence back in the language you’re speaking: “Oh, you’re thirsty? I’ll get you some water.”
  • Give them the phrases they need in advance. “Can I go to the toilet?”, “I don’t understand” and “Can I play with you?” in the language of the nursery or school take away a lot of fear in the first weeks.
  • Read aloud in the home language. Books bring words that never come up in everyday chat.
  • Look after the roots. Calls with grandparents, family celebrations, songs and stories aren’t “extra work”: they’re what connects your child to the family.

Every version of {{play|Chatterbox}} – English, Russian and Portuguese – has a My languages section for children who grow up in several languages. It appears when a child has two or more languages in their profile. You can choose from Russian, Ukrainian, Portuguese, English, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Hebrew, Turkish and Chinese.

  • One sound, many languages: how the same sound is made in each of your child’s languages, with words to listen to and say.
  • Say it in all your languages: a picture and its name in each of your child’s languages; your child listens to each word and says it too.
  • Guess the language: your child hears a word and works out which language it was.

The voices come from your phone or tablet: if it has no voice for one of the languages, the game tells you.

If your family speaks Russian, the Russian version has three more games in this section for now: the child’s own language map (which language at home, with the grandparents, at school or nursery, with friends and out and about); a game where the child picks the language for a person and a situation – “tell the teacher: can I go to the toilet?” – then hears the phrase and says it; and everyday phrases for nursery, school and the playground in Portuguese, English, German, Spanish, French, Italian and Ukrainian, plus the family’s own phrases to practise. They aren’t in the English version yet.

Whether English is your child’s home language or the language of school, the English version practises English sounds and early reading: see our guides to {{page:r|the R sound}}, {{page:l|the L sound}}, {{page:s|S, Z and SH}} and {{page:read|learning to read with phonics}}. And grandparents in another country can join with the family login (one login and a password of 4 pictures): they see what the grandchildren did this week, send them praise and play chess with them. More in {{page:grand|Chatterbox for grandparents}}.

Mixing languages, an accent and a silent period at a new nursery are no cause for alarm. It’s worth seeing a speech and language therapist (SLT) if the difficulties show in all of your child’s languages, not only the new one: your child says little and struggles to understand both at home and at nursery, or even close family find them hard to understand. If you can, look for a specialist who works with bilingual children.

Chatterbox is home practice, not a diagnosis and not a replacement for a specialist.

faq.q: Won’t my child get confused if we speak three languages?
faq.a: No. Children who grow up in several languages work out over time which language goes where. Mixing languages when they speak is a normal part of that journey, not confusion.

faq.q: I speak our home language, but my child answers in the school language. What should I do?
faq.a: Don’t scold, and don’t pretend you don’t understand. Calmly keep speaking your language and say your child’s idea back in it. The more real things there are to do in the home language – conversations, books, games, calls to Grandma – the more willingly your child will speak it.

faq.q: Can being bilingual make a child start talking later?
faq.a: Bilingualism on its own doesn’t cause a speech delay. If your child says little in all of their languages, see a speech and language therapist – don’t wait in the hope that it’s “just the languages” and will pass.

faq.q: Which languages do the My languages games work with?
faq.a: Chatterbox itself is in English, Russian and Portuguese, and all three versions have the My languages section. In it you can choose Russian, Ukrainian, Portuguese, English, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Hebrew, Turkish and Chinese. The language map, the game about who to say what to and the everyday phrases are only in the Russian version for now.
